newsitem.title: PERU: Peru and rebels agree to open hostage negotiations.
newsitem.headline: Peru and rebels agree to open hostage negotiations.

text.p: The Peruvian government and Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima agreed at a meeting on Tuesday to open negotiations to end the 56-day siege.

The second-in-command of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), Rolly Rojas, and President Alberto Fujimori's negotiator Domingo Palermo, met for four hours at a nearby Red Cross safe house to hammer out conditions for talks to bring the tense standoff to an end.

After a Red Cross car transported Rojas, known by the nom de guerre "El Arabe" (The Arab), the 150 feet (50 metres) back to the besieged residence, Vatican mediator Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani and Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent told reporters that both sides had agreed to further dialogue.

"Today we began the preliminary conversations. We have agreed the procedures to follow in future conversations and we have agreed to continue the conversations at a date yet to be set," said Vincent, translating Cipriani's statement.

Tuesday's talks, mediated by the Red Cross, the Vatican, Canada and an observer from Japan, were the first time the MRTA and government had met face-to-face since Education Minister Palermo met MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini on Dec. 28.

The siege began on Dec. 17 when 15 MRTA rebels stormed the residence during a cocktail party and seized more than 500 guests. They freed most but kept 72 hostages, including two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and Fujimori's brother.
Japan has taken an intense interest in the siege and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto met Fujimori, who is the son of Japanese immigrants, in Canada to urge a peaceful solution.

Japanese Foreign Ministry spokesman Hiroshi Hashimoto said in Tokyo on Tuesday: "We hope the talks will pave the way for the start of full negotiations so that the incident can be solved peacefully, and the hostages freed early."

Fujimori, expected home on Wednesday from a trip to London, told Peruvian reporters accompanying him "there are elements that give us a certain optimism. (Rojas) is a sociologist familiar with the theme and he could help us find a solution."
He expects the talks with Rojas, a 34-year-old former transport worker who joined the MRTA while at university, to lead to formal negotiations in the next few weeks with Cerpa.

Fujimori's refusal to consider the rebels' main demand -- the release of about 400 comrades from Peruvian jails -- had stymied earlier attempts at dialogue. He is sticking to his hard line, telling a news conference in London: "Definitely the Peruvian government is not going to pay any ransom."
He is open, however, to the possibility of asylum abroad for the hostage takers and suggested Cuba might take them.

Cerpa Cartolini's latest comments also show negotiations are unlikely to be a pushover. "The beginning of talks does not necessarily mean the start of a solution to the conflict," he said by walkie-talkie from inside the residence on Monday, accusing Fujimori of using the talks as a "psychological weapon" and of making a "veiled threat" to use force.

With tension around the residence high on Tuesday after the rebels tossed out a grenade and fired shots on Monday to ward off police, special forces reinforced the security cordon in nearby streets and put extra sharpshooters on nearby roofs.
